questions.question_text: A Vermont landlord refuses to rent to a 22-year-old applicant solely because of the applicant's age. Under Vermont fair housing law, is this lawful?
questions.correct_answer: No, age 18+ is a protected class in VT
distractors: Yes, age is not a protected class
Yes, if the tenant is under 25
No, but only for buyers, not renters
questions.explanation: Age is a protected class under 9 V.S.A. § 4503, and federal fair housing law has no age class at all. Vermont's only age-related carve-outs are refusing to rent to a person under the age of majority (§ 4504(3)) and qualified senior housing (62+, or 55+ communities meeting the statutory tests) under § 4503(b).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a protected class under Vermont fair housing law but NOT under federal fair housing law?
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4503 protects race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, marital status, religious creed, color, national origin, and disability, and separately protects people who intend to occupy a dwelling with minor children, who receive public assistance, and who are victims of abuse, sexual assault, or stalking. Receipt of public assistance — which covers Section 8 vouchers — has no federal counterpart.

questions.question_text: A Vermont property manager tells an applicant that victims of domestic violence are too risky as tenants. This statement violates Vermont law because it discriminates based on what?
questions.explanation: Vermont fair housing law specifically protects victims of abuse, sexual assault, and stalking from housing discrimination. Refusing to rent based on this status is unlawful.

questions.question_text: A Vermont seller refuses to negotiate with a buyer because the buyer is in a civil union. Which protected class does this violate?
questions.explanation: Marital status is a protected class under Vermont fair housing law. Discrimination based on civil union status falls under this protection. Vermont recognizes both civil unions and marriages.

questions.question_text: A Vermont listing agent tells a seller they can reject offers from applicants using housing vouchers. Is this accurate?
questions.correct_answer: No, source of income is protected in VT
distractors: Yes, sellers can choose any buyer
Yes, if the property is owner-occupied
questions.explanation: Vermont protects receipt of public assistance under 9 V.S.A. § 4503, so a blanket refusal to deal with voucher holders is unlawful in a covered transaction. Note the limits: § 4504 exempts only the RENTAL of a dwelling in an owner-occupied building of three or fewer units — it does not exempt sales.

questions.question_text: A Vermont landlord lives in one unit of a two-unit building and refuses a Section 8 voucher holder for the other unit. Under 9 V.S.A. § 4504, is the refusal covered by state fair housing law?
questions.correct_answer: No — owner-occupied buildings of three or fewer units are exempt from the rental provisions
distractors: Yes — Vermont has no owner-occupied exemption of any kind
Yes — the exemption covers only single-family homes
Yes — the exemption applies only to familial status
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4504(2) provides that the § 4503 provisions relating to the rental of a dwelling do not apply if the unit is in a building with three or fewer units and the owner or a member of the owner's immediate family resides in one of them. The advertising rule in § 4503(a)(3) still applies, and federal protections against racial discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 1982 are never waived — but Vermont's exemption is real, and it is narrower than the federal four-unit 'Mrs. Murphy' rule.

questions.question_text: A Vermont apartment complex advertises units as 'professionals only, no voucher holders.' Which Vermont fair housing provision does this violate?
questions.explanation: Advertising 'no voucher holders' violates Vermont's receipt-of-public-assistance protection, and 9 V.S.A. § 4503(a)(3) bars discriminatory notices, statements, and advertisements. The advertising rule applies even to landlords who otherwise qualify for the owner-occupied exemption in § 4504(2).

questions.question_text: Vermont fair housing law prohibits discrimination in which of the following activities?
questions.explanation: Vermont fair housing law broadly covers sale, rental, and financing of housing. Prohibited practices include discrimination in advertising, showing properties, negotiating terms, and setting conditions.

questions.question_text: A Vermont landlord sets different lease terms for tenants receiving public assistance versus those with employment income. Is this lawful?
questions.correct_answer: No, terms cannot vary by income source
distractors: Yes, if the rent amount is the same
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4503(a)(2) prohibits discriminating in the terms, conditions, or privileges of a rental because of a protected characteristic, and receipt of public assistance is protected. Unless the landlord falls within a § 4504 exemption, tenants using vouchers must be offered the same lease terms as anyone else.

questions.question_text: Which statement about Vermont's fair housing exemptions is correct?
questions.correct_answer: Vermont's owner-occupied exemption covers buildings of three or fewer units
distractors: Vermont recognizes no owner-occupied exemption at all
Vermont's owner-occupied exemption matches the federal four-unit rule
Vermont exempts all owner-occupied single-family home sales
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4504(2) exempts the rental of a dwelling in a building of three or fewer units where the owner or a member of the owner's immediate family lives in one of them — one unit tighter than the federal four-unit 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption, and limited to rentals. Section 4504 also exempts refusing to rent to a minor, legitimate business practices such as reference checks, and certain religious organizations.

questions.question_text: A tenant believes a Vermont landlord discriminated based on gender identity. To which state agency should the tenant file a complaint?
questions.explanation: The Vermont Human Rights Commission investigates housing discrimination complaints under 9 V.S.A. ch. 141. If it finds reasonable grounds it may pursue conciliation or bring suit in Superior Court seeking damages, penalties, attorney's fees, and injunctive relief.

questions.question_text: Within what time period must a fair housing complaint be filed with the Vermont Human Rights Commission?
questions.explanation: A housing discrimination complaint should be filed with the Vermont Human Rights Commission within one year of the alleged discriminatory act — the same one-year window HUD applies to federal Fair Housing Act complaints. A complainant may instead bring a private action in Vermont Superior Court.

questions.question_text: After investigating a fair housing complaint, the Vermont Human Rights Commission may issue which type of order?
questions.explanation: The Vermont Human Rights Commission investigates, pursues conciliation, and — where it finds reasonable grounds — may seek cease and desist relief, damages, and civil penalties through Superior Court. It has no criminal jurisdiction and no authority over real estate licenses, which belong to the Real Estate Commission.

questions.question_text: A prevailing complainant in a Vermont fair housing lawsuit in Superior Court may recover which of the following?
questions.explanation: A prevailing complainant in a Vermont fair housing case filed in Superior Court may recover actual damages, attorney fees, and other appropriate relief as determined by the court.

questions.question_text: Besides filing with the Vermont Human Rights Commission, a housing discrimination victim may also pursue a claim through which court?
questions.explanation: Victims of housing discrimination in Vermont may file a complaint with the VHRC or bring a private lawsuit directly in Vermont Superior Court. Both options allow recovery of damages and attorney fees.
